blocks.x: I'll make a note on here first that we're interviewing Mr. Andrew Morgan over at the record store 731 St. Peter and this is Bill Russell and the date is July the 4th, the holiday, 1961. Could you give your full name? Do you have a middle name?
No, my name is Andrew Morgan.
Can you tell us just where you were born? Was it here in the city?
Well, I wasn't born in the city of New Orleans. I was born down in Florida.
Over in Florida? Yeah.
So down in Pensacola. But I was raised up here in the city of New Orleans.
What was the date of your birth, if you don't mind?
I was born 1901 on the 13th day of March.
March. How much older was your brother Sam and Isaiah about? How many other members of the family were there too? I knew, of course, your youngest.

Well, I'm not the youngest brother, you see. Well, it was Sam. He was the oldest one. Then my brother Robert, he died. And I have another brother, Isaiah. And I came, a brother next to you, Isaiah. And come a brother, Albert, the bass player. He was much younger than the master. He was much younger than me, yeah. And I had another brother, but he didn't play music. He was the six of us that I could remember.
Did your father play any instruments?
Well, my daddy wasn't a musician, but he was a great song singer. He used to sing in the church, jubilee songs and different things.
What church denomination was it? Baptist? My father was Baptist, yeah.
Did your mother sing or play anything?
Did your mother sing or play anything?
My mother, she was Baptist too. Did she sing in the choir? She was a steward sister of the church. And my daddy, he would just used to sing, you know, jubilee songs.
I forgot where the, was your brother Isaiah born in Florida too?

No, I think Isaiah was born in Louisiana. Sam probably too. He was in Louisiana. My brother Robert was born in Louisiana. I think it was only one or two of us was born in Florida, but I just don't, I think it was the brother that died because my daddy was a man that bleed trees, you know, do timber work and different things like that. And he was always there. So he traveled around. Traveled around.

You see. What was about the earliest music you can remember? Was it the people singing around Homer? Do you remember any bands or anything when you were a little, almost, say, four or five years old or anything like that? Can you remember what the music was like when you
first heard? No, no, I couldn't think of nothing. Well, my brother used to have a band when I was quite a young fella, you see. My brother Sam, he had a brass band.
Was that over here then? You were living in?
Well, we were living in Louisiana at that time. You moved back here then? Yeah. Well, they had a band they called the Magnolia Band.
Oh, yes. I've heard of it.
And I'm going to see if I can think of some of the fellas that used to play with them.
Yeah, if you can remember.

Well, Sam, he was playing trumpet. And his clarinet player was Joe Watson. Then Alfred William used to play with him. Oh, yeah. The drummer. And T-Boy, I can't think of T-Boy's last name, but I know they did call him T-Boy. He was the bass player.
Bass, yeah. Well, I never knew him except T-Boy Ramay. You know, the trumpet player used to be in the
United States. Yeah, no, this is another T-Boy. And Yank used to play trombone with him.
Yank Johnson.
Yeah, Yank Johnson. Well then, my brother played around the city here for quite a while.
About what date was that, can you remember in relation to the First World War, was that
the war? Around 1918. Around 1918, yes. Because they used to play all out around the fairground, different places at West End. Yeah.
And... What was West End like in those days? Did they have a park? I've seen the old pictures where they have a bandstand and the hotels and everything. Where did they play?

Well, they used to have a bandstand. Mostly they played Dixland music, you know. And they used to have trolley cars ride up. Yeah, I remember that. Yeah. I remember that, yeah. Then they had a little old train down here on the Legendfield Street. We used to call it the Smokey Marys.
Oh yeah, I've heard of that.
Yeah.
The Mellonbury.

Yeah, you used to go at the Mellonbury. Yeah. And they used to have a pavilion out there. They called Manual Pavilion. And my brother used to play out there. That was even time of Buddy Petit time and Louis Armstrong.
I was wondering a little more about the West End. I never did know much whether... Did they have camps out there? They played over the water or were they night clubs?
Well, they did. They played on the water in camps at the West End and also down at Mellonbury.

I remember. Same type of thing. I wondered if any bands ever played out in that park, you know, where they had a bandstand, like if that was for brass band concerts I heard they used to give there. Do you remember anything like that?

No, I don't remember nothing like that. But I remember several brass bands that they had around the city of New Orleans when I was quite a youngster coming up. They had Excelsa brass band and they had Tuxedas brass band. That was time of Papa Celestans. And had the Imperial brass band. Another brass band that I knew, Silverleaf. All that was around Bunk Johnson them times.
Do you remember who were in some of those bands, like the Excelsior, who the leader was?

Well, I don't know who was the leader of the Excelsior, but I did remember some of the fellows that used to play Eno's band. I think Manuel Perez, he was a trumpet player. I know Tuxedas, that was Papa Celestans. And Ada Jackson. The trubor player. Yeah, the sousaphone player. And I just can't think of who I was in the band at the time, but I remember the band when I was quite a young fellow. Now then after late years, then come the Eureka brass band. Well, at that time, I had a fellow playing in that band by the Willie Wilson.
I never knew him. What did he play?
Trumpet. I didn't remember that. Yeah. Never heard of him, huh?
Well, maybe, but I don't remember.
Well then, at that time, Ray had the Eureka band. He used to play trombone. Yeah, I remember
he told us about that.
And in this band, Willie Webber used to play trumpet. Jack August used to play saxophone. And I did play the clarinet. Yeah, E-flat clarinet.
I was going to ask you, we might as well get back to that, just when you first took up music, what you started on, and about how old you were.

Oh, when I started out with music, I was about, I guess about 22, 23 years old. Well, you didn't start when you were a little boy then? No, no. I thought with all those musicians in the family, you might have started doing it. Well, no. I was a man when I started trombone this year. Really? I was married when I was taking up music.
Did you ever fool with the instruments when you were a kid though, to blow on your brother's carnet or anything?

Well, no. I never tried to play the carnet, but my brother Isaiah, he did. And after my brother Isaiah started playing music, well then that encouraged me to take up the clarinet. That was your first instrument then? Yeah, my first instrument. And the first clarinet that I bought to start playing on, I bought it from Albert Nicholson.
Oh, yeah.
A clarinet player. Well, he used to play with my brother Sam sometime. And...
What kind of an instrument was it? Albert?
It was Albert's system. Same instrument that I play now, Albert. And out goes the old man Sharleneen, I've taken lessons with old man Sharleneen. I guess you heard of him.
I've heard of him, never got to know him though.
And now, I've taken lessons with Pinchback Two Row. You heard of him?
Oh, yes. I've heard of him. Had a brass band.

Had a brass band. And he had charge of the WPA band too some time back. And now, I've taken a few lessons with David Jones. Oh, yeah. I was on tenor saxophone. And I come in to play any different little bands. Well, our first band was then, if I'm not making a mistake, it's the Imperial. Well, Jack August was playing alto saxophone. I was playing the clarinet. Willie Webber was playing trumpet. And Dr. Bechier, who was that? Oh, yeah. He played trombone? Oh, he was playing trombone. I knew him very well. Yeah. Well, then we played together for a while and we had a bass player by the name of Hudson. Yeah, that's been there, yeah. Oh. Well, that's been quite a while back. I think he's dead. Then after I started playing, then Arthur Durdne came into the band. He was a trumpet player. Me, Arthur Durdne, Whitney Arsenault, Whitney Arsenault, and Whitney Arsenault, and Dr. Bechier. Then I can't think of the drummer that we had playing, but I remember when Kid Howard came to the band. He played drums. Yeah, he played drums. I would come and play drum with us a while. Then after that, my brother, Isaiah, he had a little band he called Young Morgan. Yeah. I've heard that I never did get
that straight. It wasn't that part of Sam's band. Yeah. Well, that's before we joined the band

with Sam. So, my brother was playing up here on Liberty Street. I just forget the name of the place. But anyway, well, Jim Robison was in the band. In your little band? Yeah. And that's Young Morgan. Yeah, the young one. Sidney Brown, that was the bass player. And Johnny Deve was playing banjo. No, I think we had at that time on the drum, Rudolph. I just can't think of Rudolph's last name.

Is that Bollier? Bollier? Bollier, that's, yeah. Big Rudolph. Yeah. So, um... He'd been sick, had a stroke some time ago. Well, that's what I heard. But we interviewed him about a month ago, and he looks in pretty good health. So, he'd like to play again now. That's good. And they'd be able to start in again.

So, uh, he and this Young Morgan band, well, Jim Robison had a brother they called Sam. I've heard of him, but never got to know him. Well, that's the fellow that I take in his place, you see. Uh, seems like, uh, that they had heard me play, and they're, uh, they're like my style of playing. And then I joined the band. So then I played with Young Morgan around here for a few years. And after my brother Sam, he was sick, and, uh, he was not able to keep up a band by himself. So then he came over to my brother Isaiah band, Young Morgan, and he taken over. So then, uh, the three brothers was playing together then. So then, uh...
And he still called it then the Sam Morgan band?
Then the name was Sam Morgan's band. Well, then, uh, we played around the city of Diorleans.
Was he the leader then of it? Did he...
Sam was the leader. The real leader. Yeah, he taken over. Really took over and directed him over.
He taken over, yeah. And that's why... Stopped off and did all the... I don't know if Isaiah maybe did that sometime?
Isaiah was playing second trumpet.
He was playing something.

And, uh, Jim Robison, Sidney Brown, John O'Dea, Rudolph played a while, and after, uh, they got rid of Rudolph. And, uh, boy, they called Shine Kim in the band. Now, Nolan Williams was his name. Oh, it was. I guess you heard that name. That's right. Jim Robison has a picture.
That's right.
Of your band. Well, he was the one, he was the one who made the cut with us.
The one who made the records on Columbia. Yeah.

Well, a long while after that, then, um, he was a fella, I don't know, they couldn't get along with him. And then there, this boy, Roy Evans, he came to the band. He played with Sam. And I think he played with Sam until Sam had given up playing music. He died. Sam died. And after that, this boy, he died too. So from that on, I played around the city of New Orleans with different fellows. I played with Kit Howard's band after he had a band. And I played with, uh, George Williams' band. The drummer.
The drummer.
Drummer, yes. And, uh.

Well, I was going to ask some more about your lessons, um, because naturally we're interested in some of these real old timers like Chaline and I didn't get, never, we'll never get to talk to him of course. Old man Chaline? Yeah, anything that you can tell us about your lessons? Did he use a regular method book? Do you remember what it was?
Well, yeah, we used to use, uh, an auto language at that time, you see. And I'd taken lessons with him through the auto language on a clarinet.
Um, how much did he charge for lessons? Do you remember?

Well, he was only charging, uh, a half a dollar for lessons. How often did you go? Once a week or twice? Well, then we could go, no, we was, we were taking lessons twice a week with him. Twice a week. Twice a week with him. That was the price, Ron, you know, on lessons at that time. 50 cents. 50 cents. So, Joe Watson, he gave me a lesson on the clarinet, well he didn't charge me anything. Pinchback Churro, well I paid him a half a dollar. David Jones, it was a half a dollar. And, Ennis Band, and Earl Fosch here used to play saxophone with us, with Sam Morgan's band.
Harold Dejan's always talking about him, he's wonderful. Yeah.

He's a wonderful saxophone player. Well then he gave me a lot of ideas about playing the tenor saxophone, because he showed my old fingering on the saxophone, and him and I used to sit down and play duets together. Well then, I played with some of that. For sure.
I was going to ask about Chalney again. Somebody told me, maybe it was Harold Dejan, I think, took some lessons from him. Or what's it, Brother Cornbread or something, you know, the clarinetist.
Well, Brother Cornbread used to take lessons with old man Chalney. Him and I was a scholar over there, because he had a very large place, and he had just so many youngsters.
Maybe he said he had a band, didn't he?

Well, we did have a big brass band. He had a brass band, but all of his pupils. Yeah, and he put all of the boys on a big truck on Sundays, and sometimes fellas would give dances and they wasn't able to pay the band that was going to play the dance for the advertising. Well then he used to come and get Chalney's band, and maybe we'd have about thirty of us a big truck to go around the city of New Orleans and advertise for the dance that there was going to be on a Sunday night or either that Monday night.

I'm trying to think there was some brass band they told me about, maybe connected to St. Catherine's Hall or something up there. Was that, that wouldn't be your band? Well, uh. Maybe the school they had, you know, the Church Cross and Charity Hospital had that big hall, and they had a school there. I'm trying to think if it wasn't Chalney then had that.
No, no. Somebody else told me that. The only band, a big band that I played in around that neighborhood, well we used to go and rehearse, so every day that was the WPA band.
Well, you were in the WPA band?
Yeah, I played in the WPA band. You might have seen one of my, seen my pictures.
Yes, I've seen those pictures. Yeah.
Well we had from close around 119. About everybody in town was in that.
Yeah. I don't know who was in the picture, but I remember an awful lot of people.

Well I stayed, I stayed in that band until we cut the band on to 19 pieces at that time. Now we used to rehearse over at the Tulane's Club, and we used to rehearse a lot here on, about the Fifth Ward Club out here on Dumaine Street.
Yeah, somebody told us, I know Kid Clayton told me they worked over there. I never knew that.
Yeah, just on Dumaine near Charter Street. Near Charter, is that what even? Between Charter and Decatur.
What sort of a place was it then?
Well it used to be a, Atlanta club, you know, boxing and different things. Oh yeah. Yeah. They called that the Fifth Ward Club. Yeah.
It's not there now I guess then.
Well that was during the WPA time.
I mean, yeah.

Well then I played around the city. I played with D.D. and Billy a while, and Ernest Rogers, and I played with, that was during the WPA time. I played, I played a job with Bunk Johnson and George Lewis.

Well I remember hearing down the country violin. Yeah. I remember later Bunk said he'd like for you to be, wish you could have gone to New York and played with him once. Yeah. So you told me that one time. He'd like to use you on clarinet.
Well then I played around Boydman Street. Played out there with Bill Matthews. And continued on playing with Bill Matthews now when he had dates, you know. Yeah.
I remember hearing you at the paddock quite often there.
Yeah, I played at the paddock.
Some nights you'd be there on the Tuesday night when they'd take a night off, you'd be there quite regularly for a long time.

Yeah, well, I played at the paddock with Bill Matthews and I played there with Thomas Jefferson. And I played at the paddock with Freddie Coleman and we left the paddock and went down to the Mardi Gras. Played down at the Mardi Gras with Freddie Coleman. You're a member of his band then.
I forgot that. Were you there quite a while at the Mardi Gras then?
Yeah. Yeah. I worked there just about, maybe about a month or about six weeks in there or something like that. And I played at the Mardi Gras with Kid Howard's band on Tuesday night.
Yeah, I remember that.
So then I played with Kid Thomas band a long time too. I played with Kid Thomas, Elton, Joe James, and I think Twatnam is... Butler I believe.
Butler, yeah.
Is it Joseph Butler?
Joseph Butler.
That's right. We haven't interviewed him yet.
He's a hard one to catch up with too.
I think he works over there across the street on Sunday with Kid Thomas.
Yeah, he was here, he's been here a couple of times the last couple of weeks.

Yeah, well I worked with Kid Thomas from 1936 up until about 1940 or 1942. You know, on Saturdays we used to go all down to Bay and play around Raceland and down at the top of the hill. We used to play it off and play out around Grand Island. Put it right down there. Yeah.
I always hear about mosquitoes when they tell them about that.

Oh they had plenty of mosquitoes. I seen the time we played out there they had to put up a mosquito ball for the band, to keep the mosquitoes from biting the band so we could give the satisfaction to the people that was dancing.

Well while I think of it, the other couple weeks ago we were over across the river taking pictures of all the old halls. Professor Minetta went around with us, Ralph and I. We took pictures of the old places like the Ping Pong on Brooklyn Street. That was probably before your time, back 1905 Eden Fess used to hear music there. But then we wondered about some of those later halls and we went over there near your section I guess where the Elks have their place.
Oh you're talking about the.
And then up near the pumping station over.
I think that was the Casinos if I'm not making a mistake.

I'm wondering what other clubs were there. What was the name of them? I can't even think now at all. I know them very well. The club up when they tore down when they built the bridge. What's the matter? I can't think of those. At the Young Men's huh? No, not the Young Men's.
I'll think of it if I don't try so hard in a minute.
But wasn't there another club there near where the Elks are now? At that corner? No, well I don't know.
Do you remember any other clubs over in there? Well all the clubs that I knew over there was the Elks and I knew the Young Men's of Algea, the Young Men's of McDonaville and they have the Wolf.
Yeah the Wolf and then Gretney.
Yeah they up in Gretney. No, I don't know any other clubs that organized over the river. Nothing no more in the Masonic.
I can't even think of it. It wasn't the Eagles but it was something like...
The Eagle Eye Hall?
Eagle Eye, yeah. Yeah, Eagle Eye Hall.

Is that the one they tore down? Oh yeah, that was just on the line there. Well the Elks you still have them eating there too at Eagle Eye Hall. That's just on the line where the New Orleans and Algea's bridge comes across the river. Well I remember that because I played in that place with Kit Thomas several times.

I have some of those pictures I think I have wrote down on the back of one of them. See if I can find the name of that. The Green Hall. I don't think that's so much junk here it can't even pick it up. The Alisons have already passed. We're going to have to go there. I was going to ask some more. I'll be looking for this but it's going to take me ten minutes to find it.
To find it, yeah.

There's thousands of things in this one box here I think. Pictures and clippings. Anyway, I'm going to ask some more about the Sam Morgan band. Oh yeah, well. One thing while I think of it about the slapstick. I've heard they, was it your brother Sam or Isaiah? Which one used the slapstick?
Sam, he used to use the slapstick. Another box of photographs. And then I'll be trying.
Sam had a wonderful band around y'all.
Because it was all the talk of Sam Morgan band. band, and he composed a few records. I wanted to ask some more about the records,
the date when you made that. If you don't remember the exact date, I know it's hard to remember the exact date, but I mean, where were they made and about when?

I think those records were made out here on Canal Street at the old Gotchers building on Canal and Charter, and I think that was in the year around 1927, if I'm not making a mistake. Yeah, around 26 or 27.
Most of the budgets in that picture, I guess, were in the, made the records, is that right? Remember that picture, I know Jim Robinson has one, it's been printed in one of the books someplace.
The picture that Jim Robinson had? Yeah, he has it up on his wall. Well, I have one of those pictures too. Well, I know every member of the band was at that time.
Was that the same group then that made the record about that time?

Yes. In the picture? Yes. Every one of those men was in that picture, but we didn't have the piano player with us in that picture when we made the record. Because one of the records was Walter DeCue, he made one of the record with us, one or two.
Then we had another. I forgot Walter DeCue was on that then.

Yeah, he's on the record, yes. Then we had another boy by the name of Tink. Oh yeah, is he the piano player? Piano player. Those were the only two piano players that made those records with Sam. But the rest of the men's is the men's that you've seen that made the records. It was the men's that was on this picture. No. I think Roy made, if I'm not making a mistake, Roy was playing the drum with us at the time we had made those records. Roy Evans.
I found the sheet I was looking for, but it doesn't have the name of that place on. I was trying to think of the name of the hall.
Name of the hall across where you used to it?
Yeah, near the Elks. We're over on Elmira, in the 1200 block of Elmira.
I think that was the Cassianers, if I'm not making a...

Yeah, okay. There's still another name that Fess told us and somebody else had mentioned once too. Kid Thomas mentioned the name of the hall over there and it's still one we haven't mentioned yet. I just can't think of it. It's in my mind, but I just can't get a hold of it.
This hall, I'm trying to think now because... Around Elmira there. It was on Elmira Street. At that time, if I'm not making a mistake, Mr. Russell, it was the Casinos.
Casinos.
Yeah. You may ask Kid Thomas about that because I played several dances there with Thomas Mann at the time.
Was it on a corner or in the middle of the block?
It was just about the second house from the corner. Upstairs.
Upstairs.
Yeah.
Some of the other things that we took pictures of were the Manhattan Saloon of Newton and Teche. Do you remember when it was the Manhattan Saloon? It's...
Well, I would have been, but I...
That's before your time over there too, I guess.
Yeah. Yeah, it was because I've been living over the river now just about... I've been living over there about seven going into the eight years now. So I moved over then.
Do you remember a place called Elmira Pleasure Ground? No. Or Perseverance Pleasure Ground. It used to be up where that pumping station is in there now.
No, I don't know very much about over there because...
When did you move over there by the way?
In 53. Well, you only moved over in 53. Yeah.
I thought maybe you lived there for years.
No, no. I used to live here in the city of New Orleans. Over in here. Yeah. Because several of you men came by my house when I was living on 919 St. Peter Street. Yeah.
And you wouldn't have known all of these old places then that...
No, I don't know very many old places over in Algea or Gretany.
There were some places like the Pythian Hall and the Alhambra Club that Fess told us about.

No, I think that was before my time. It was before your time. Now, I'll tell you a fellow you might get a little information on it. Peter Bocca. Yes, Peter would know. Yeah. Either Manuel Mineta or Kit Thomas.
Yeah, well, the Fess told us this several things. We were just wondering about a couple of places we weren't sure of there.
Uh-huh.
I was going to ask some more about the Sam Morgan band. Whose idea was it, that slapstick of ever using that? Did he get that from the drummer or something? Or how did he happen to start on that?

Well, at that time the drummers used to use slapsticks in the band. And Sam was, had been very sick and I guess that was something he thought would, you could bring Newt to the band, you understand? Maybe not as far as I missed the story. Yeah, no, when the band was playing he used to use that stick. Yeah. And I saw some time back, and Bebe Ridley, he used to use that stick too. Oh, he did? Yeah, when he was playing drums. I know he was playing trombone at that time. Well, Sam used that stick a long time, I'm telling you. The band be playing, Sam reached down there and get that stick, put his trumpet down, and he'd get that stick, man. And keep the time with the stick. Yeah. Sam is the drummer's keeping time.
Kid Thomas uses that quite a bit nowadays too. Who? Kid Thomas still has a slapstick. Oh yeah. He used it. Manuel Paul sometimes too.
Yeah, I'm quite sure he did because when I was playing with him, he used to have a slapstick.
Yeah, they usually hit it on the after beat.
Yeah, on the after beat. Well, Sam had a good band around the city of New Orleans and everybody. Everybody raves about it. Everybody. Yeah, they really talk about Sam Morgan's band.
Where did you all play mostly? Any certain favorite halls?

Well, yes, we used to play up on Ramport Street at that store every Sunday night. And we used to play at the Center Center's Club, played at the Economy Hall, played at the Corporate Hall, and we used to play at a little place called the San Su.
Oh yes, that was up on the Hall. The Hall.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
You were talking about the...
Someone at you.
You were talking about San Boyd's band.
There were several places that we had been playing.
Oh, the San Sioux Hall, you mentioned.
Yeah, we used to play at the San Sioux, then we used to play at the Bulls Club.
Where was the San Sioux Hall? I think they just tore that down lately. Was it in back or up by the front of the street?
It used to be into the back. You had to go... Go back to... Yeah.
It wasn't right on the street.
It wasn't right on the street.
